canonical_statement: The study aimed to estimate the impact of changes in chlamydia treatment policy on recurrent/persistent rectal Chlamydia trachomatis infections among men who have sex with men at the PHSKC Sexual Health Clinic.
A secondary objective was to identify demographic and behavioral correlates of azithromycin receipt before and after the clinic changed rectal chlamydia prescribing guidelines.

The controlled interrupted time-series population included men who have sex with men who tested positive and were treated for rectal chlamydia or rectal gonorrhea at the PHSKC Sexual Health Clinic from January 1, 2012 through December 31, 2024.

population.label: MSM treated for rectal CT or rectal GC at PHSKC SHC, 2012-2024
inclusion_criteria: Positive and treated for rectal CT or rectal GC at PHSKC SHC

canonical_statement: The azithromycin-correlate analysis included MSM with a rectal chlamydia diagnosis and excluded rectal gonorrhea co-infections and cases prescribed both azithromycin and doxycycline.

population.label: Rectal CT cases used for azithromycin-correlate analysis
inclusion_criteria: MSM with a rectal CT diagnosis

canonical_statement: The PHSKC Sexual Health Clinic changed its rectal chlamydia protocol beginning in April 2016 to recommend exclusively doxycycline.

concept.text: Doxycycline-only rectal CT treatment protocol

canonical_statement: Before the 2021 national guideline change, CDC guidance listed doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days or azithromycin 1 g once as first-line chlamydia treatments.

concept.text: Azithromycin
Doxycycline

canonical_statement: The primary analysis used a controlled interrupted time-series design with segmented regression and rectal gonorrhea recurrence/persistence as a control outcome.
The cITS analysis defined pre-implementation as January 2012-June 2016, implementation as July 2016-September 2021, and fully implemented as October 2021-December 2024.
The primary recurrent/persistent rectal chlamydia outcome was a second rectal chlamydia NAAT diagnosis 14-90 days after an initial diagnosis.

concept.text: Recurrent/persistent rectal Chlamydia trachomatis infection

outcome.definition: Second rectal CT NAAT diagnosis 14-90 days after an initial diagnosis

canonical_statement: The control recurrent/persistent rectal gonorrhea outcome was a second rectal gonorrhea NAAT diagnosis 14-90 days after an initial diagnosis.

concept.text: Recurrent/persistent rectal Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection

outcome.definition: Second rectal GC NAAT diagnosis 14-90 days after an initial diagnosis

canonical_statement: The study definition of recurrent/persistent infection combined reinfections with persistent infections because the EHR data could not distinguish the two scenarios.
Recurrent/persistent infections were aggregated by calendar quarter; rectal CT/GC co-infections were counted in both outcome groups and comprised 2.3% of RP infections.
The primary cITS model was a negative binomial model with quarterly indicators for seasonality and an offset for the quarterly number of individuals with rectal CT or GC.

Potential time-varying confounders were screened with generalized linear models containing CT/GC, implementation period, and their interaction; age and White race met the study criterion for potential confounding.
The final cITS model was adjusted for mean age and all race groups as binary variables.

Sensitivity analyses varied the recurrent/persistent window to 14-30, 14-60, and 14-120 days; an ad hoc analysis excluded 2024 to reduce contamination from doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis rollout.
The azithromycin-correlate analysis used generalized estimating equations with a binomial family and independent correlation structure to account for repeated chlamydia cases in the same person.
The primary analysis identified 211 recurrent/persistent rectal chlamydia infections at the clinic from January 2012 through December 2024.

population.label: RP-CT infection episodes at PHSKC SHC, 2012-2024

canonical_statement: The primary analysis identified 222 recurrent/persistent rectal gonorrhea infections at the clinic from January 2012 through December 2024.

population.label: RP-GC infection episodes at PHSKC SHC, 2012-2024

canonical_statement: Median age differed across implementation periods and between RP-CT and RP-GC groups: in pre-implementation the medians were 33 and 26 years, respectively; during implementation both were 29 years; and in the fully implemented period they were 30 and 35 years.

Self-identification as White varied significantly across implementation periods and between RP-CT and RP-GC groups, with proportions ranging from 31% to 82% and a difference-in-difference p-value below 0.001.
No level-change estimate in the primary cITS analysis was statistically significant for RP-CT, RP-GC, or their relative comparison.
The 14-30-day sensitivity analysis was not reported because only one RP-CT infection occurred during the fully implemented period under that definition.
Figure 1 shows approximately parallel, increasing RP-CT and RP-GC model trends during pre-implementation.
Figure 1 shows the modeled RP-CT trend declining during clinic implementation while the RP-GC trend rises more steeply than during pre-implementation.
Figure 1 shows a steep decline in the modeled RP-CT trend after full implementation while the RP-GC trend rises after an initial drop.
After the clinic protocol change, the source reports that only about one-third of rectal CT patients received doxycycline in 2017, with doxycycline prescribing increasing to 93.1% during 2021.

The ad hoc sensitivity analysis excluding 2024 showed little change in point estimates compared with the primary analysis, but the fully implemented versus pre-implementation relative trend comparison lost statistical significance.

None of the tested patient characteristics had a statistically significant difference in their association with azithromycin receipt before versus after the guideline change; the period interaction for exchanging sex for money or drugs approached significance.

Because recurrent/persistent diagnoses required patients to return for retesting, the EHR-based outcome is subject to selection by retesting behavior, and the study could not determine the proportion of initially diagnosed patients who returned.
The study could not isolate the effect of full doxycycline-policy implementation from doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis rollout, although doxy-PEP uptake became substantial mainly in 2024.
Findings came from a single sexual health clinic and may not generalize to other settings.
The authors concluded that after the intervention was fully implemented, the trend in recurrent/persistent rectal chlamydia declined significantly relative to the rectal gonorrhea control outcome.

The discussion states that the main-model relative RP-CT versus RP-GC trend decreased by 16.9% in the fully implemented period versus the implementation period, but Table 2 and the Results assign 16.9% to fully implemented versus pre-implementation and 10.8% to fully implemented versus implementation.
The study was supported by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases through grant R01AI161019 to L.E.M.
C.M.K. reported donations of study supplies from Hologic and research support from Gilead Sciences unrelated to the submitted work.
L.E.M. reported research materials or funding from Hologic, Nabriva Therapeutics and Health Advances, and an honorarium from MedConnect.
Study data cannot be shared publicly because of participant privacy; interested parties may contact the named Public Health-Seattle & King County investigator to inquire about the data.
The University of Washington Human Subjects Division IRB approved the study and patient consent was waived.
